name: Sky Lagoon
label: Sky Lagoon
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/8685848380: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sky Lagoon'.
notes: Geothermal spa on the coast at Kópavogur.

text.description:
Sky Lagoon is a geothermal spa on the waterfront at Kársnes Harbour in Kópavogur. Construction began in early 2020 and was completed in 2021. The design takes its cues from Icelandic landscape and heritage. The palette is grey-blues, deep greens, whites and creams, and there are turf walls, a turfhouse and a plunge pool. Visitors enter through a cave tunnel that leads to the hot soaking pool. The lagoon water is kept at roughly 38 to 40 °C, so on a cool day you can expect some steam, which suits photos. Snæfellsjökull, the glacier-capped volcano, and the mountain Keilir can both be seen from the lagoon.

The phone icon on the map is about 65 m north-east of the subject. That is enough distance to take in the whole setting, with the low buildings, turf-covered edges and the sea behind them, rather than a close detail. Start with a wide shot that shows how the spa sits against the water and sky, then move in for the textures of the turf walls and the cave entrance. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines. Be considerate of bathers: frame your shots so that other guests are small or out of the picture, and check the official site before you go for any rules on photography.
text.geographic_location: Sky Lagoon is at Kársnes Harbour in Kópavogur, on the coast of south-western Iceland. Kópavogur is the town next to Reykjavik, so this is just outside the city rather than in a central district.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so check local transport options for getting to Kársnes Harbour in Kópavogur. The spa is about 1 minute on foot from there, 67 m to the south-west. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the spa and its setting. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and shoreline, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the turf walls or the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the sky or the spa is the more interesting part. Include the turf edges and the water to show the landscape-inspired design. If the weather is clear, look for Snæfellsjökull or Keilir in the distance and add them to a wide shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the spa to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or steam is washing out. If you want to capture steam drifting, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light near sunrise or sunset usually flatters the buildings and the sky. In winter, the low sun means this light lasts longer, and the spa's lighting may show up well once it gets dark, though night shots need a steady hand or night mode.

text.access_note: Sky Lagoon is a spa and is likely to be ticketed with controlled entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hallgrímskirkja
label: Hallgrímskirkja
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6184378: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hallgrímskirkja' (94 m across).
notes: Iconic church whose tower is visible across the city.

text.description:
Hallgrímskirkja is the big, pale concrete church that rises above the roofs of central Reykjavík. Its stepped tower and swept-back side wings are meant to recall the basalt columns, mountains and glaciers of the Icelandic landscape. That strong, simple outline is why it photographs so well on a phone: it stands out clearly against the sky and works as a single bold shape.

It is a Lutheran parish church, the largest church in Iceland, and at 74.5 metres tall the second tallest building in the country. It stands on the Skólavörðuholt hill and can be seen from much of the city. The church is named after the poet and cleric Hallgrímur Pétursson. Building took 41 years, from 1945 to 1986, but the steeple and wings were finished in 1974, long before the nave was consecrated.

Hold the phone upright for the tower, then turn it sideways to take in the wings. The statue of Leif Erikson stands in front of the church and can make a good foreground, although you will need to walk round to it. The church also has a lift up to a viewing deck, and its bells ring through the day, so it is worth spending a little longer here than the first photo takes.
text.geographic_location: Hallgrímskirkja stands on the Skólavörðuholt hill, near the centre of Reykjavík, and is visible from many parts of the city.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Reykjavík and head up towards the Skólavörðuholt hill, where the tower is easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower and the wings into one upright shot. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the stepped concrete columns of the spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the tower so the sides stay straight. Keep the phone level and upright so the building does not seem to lean backwards. Leave some sky above the spire. For a second shot, turn the phone sideways to include the wings, or move closer with the statue of Leif Erikson in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale concrete keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. Use Live Photos or motion if people are walking past, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the concrete shows more texture. The church can be photographed at any time of year, but check the weather first, because a clear sky shows the shape of the tower best.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship with a lift to a viewing deck, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or entry rules.

name: Icelandic Phallological Museum
label: Phallological Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1511563888: the OpenStreetMap point 'The Icelandic Phallological Museum'.
notes: Quirky museum in the city centre.

text.description:
This is the Icelandic Phallological Museum, a small and unusual museum that is as much a talking point as a photo stop. It was founded in 1997 by a retired teacher, Sigurður Hjartarson, whose collection began with a cattle whip made from a bull's penis. It spent several years in the fishing village of Húsavík, then returned to Reykjavík in 2012 under his son, Hjörtur Gísli Sigurðsson. It is on Laugavegur, the city's main shopping street. The museum has 280 specimens from 93 animal species, and the largest is the tip of a sperm whale's penis, 170 cm long. The smallest is a hamster's, only 2 mm long. Over 70,000 people are said to visit each year, so it is well known with visitors.

For a phone photo, the draw is the museum's street frontage on Laugavegur, which makes a good travel souvenir or a funny shot to send home. Shoot the outside from the pavement, keep the frame tidy and include a little of the surrounding street for context. Inside, photography rules may apply, so ask staff or check the official site before you go. The pictures below are about the outside of the building.
text.geographic_location: In central Reykjavík, on Laugavegur, the city's main shopping street.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops for this spot, so head for Laugavegur, Reykjavík's main shopping street (Laugavegur 116), and look for the museum along it. Check the official site before you go in case the address or entrance has changed. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the frontage as people see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take one shot from here, then step back along the pavement for a wider view of the whole frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges straight. Include a little of the street so the museum looks like part of the shopping street. If you want a closer detail shot of the frontage, use the telephoto (2x) rather than walking into the doorway and blocking it. Wait a moment for passers-by to clear the frame, or let one walk through for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the colours do not wash out. On an overcast day, leave the exposure as it is.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is the easiest for a clear frontage. Early in the day is usually quieter on the pavement.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but the museum itself is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry and indoor photography rules.

label: Perlan

notes: Glass dome on Öskjuhlíð hill with a viewing deck.

text.description: Perlan, also known as The Pearl, is a glass dome sitting on top of Öskjuhlíð hill, with the large hot water tanks that support it below. It photographs well because the shape is simple and easy to read: a rounded glass cap on a wide, plain base, standing on top of a hill above the city. That makes it stand out in a phone frame even from a distance. The tanks were first built in 1939 to store hot water for the city. The building opened to the public on 21 June 1991, and it now holds a museum, a planetarium, an ice cave and an observation deck. The deck looks out over Reykjavik, the surrounding mountains and the Atlantic. For a phone, the dome is the star. Stand back far enough to fit the whole curve of the glass and the tanks beneath it, and use the gridlines to keep the base level. If you can't fit everything in, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and keep the phone upright so the dome doesn't lean. Move closer for details, such as the pattern of the glass against the sky or the line where the dome meets the tanks. If you go up to the observation deck, you can also photograph the city from above, but check the official site for access and opening details before you go.
text.geographic_location: Perlan is in Reykjavik, on top of Öskjuhlíð hill. It is the building that crowns the hill.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so head for Öskjuhlíð hill, the high ground that Perlan stands on. Once you reach the hill, look for the glass dome. The phone icon on the map is on the building's mapped centre. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the dome and tanks together from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look once you step back, and the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step away from it to photograph the dome. Use the ultra-wide lens to fit it all in, or step back to gain space for a fuller view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the tanks up with a horizontal line so the building sits straight. Keep the phone upright, not tilted back, to reduce the leaning look. Leave some sky above the dome so the curve has room.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building doesn't turn into a silhouette. Try a Live Photo if clouds are moving past.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day tends to flatter the glass. At dusk, night mode can help, but rest your elbows on something steady to keep the shot sharp.

text.access_note: Check the official site for access and opening details before you go.

name: Harpa Concert Hall
label: Harpa
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/108335182: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Harpa' (143 m across).
notes: Glass-faceted concert hall on the waterfront.

text.description:
Harpa is Reykjavik's concert hall and conference centre, in the Austurhöfn area of the city. Its walls are made of glass panels in different colours and shapes, set on a steel frame. They were inspired by Iceland's basalt landscape, so the building looks a little like a block of cut crystal. It was designed by the Danish firm Henning Larsen Architects together with the artist Olafur Eliasson, and the opening concert took place on 4 May 2011. In 2013 it won the European Union's Mies van der Rohe award for contemporary architecture.

It photographs well because the façade is full of pattern. The panels pick up the sky, the water and the people walking past, so no two photos look quite the same. The façade also carries 714 LED lights, which show a video work designed by Olafur Eliasson. After dark these can add colour to your shots.

Fill the frame with the geometric panels, or use the ultra-wide lens to lean into the shape of the glass. For a wider view of the building, walk further back. Down by the water there is also a cellist sculpture called The Musician, which makes a good small foreground subject if you can reach it.
text.geographic_location: Harpa sits in the Austurhöfn area of Reykjavik.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Reykjavik and head to Harpa in the Austurhöfn area. Once you are there, the middle of the building is about 19 m to the north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) because you are so close. Switch to the default lens (1x) for cleaner, less stretched pictures of the glass, and try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a few panels as an abstract pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Take a step or two to each side to find a line of panels that you like.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the panels with them so the building does not seem to lean. Try a low angle with the ultra-wide, pointing slightly upwards, for a dramatic shot. Alternatively, zoom in on the colours and reflections for an abstract shot with no sky at all. Keep clear of passers-by or include one as a small figure for a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright panel to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky reflections do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone as still as you can, resting your elbows against your body, so the lit-up façade stays sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Low sun or the hour after sunset usually gives richer colour in the glass. Once it is dark, the lit façade makes striking night shots. Overcast days still work well for close-ups of the panels.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the surrounding area, but check the official Harpa site before you go for access to the inside and for any events or tickets.

The LED lights on the façade are most visible after dark.

name: Sun Voyager
label: Sun Voyager
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/295480918: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sun Voyager'.
notes: Steel boat sculpture on the seafront.

text.description:
Sun Voyager (Sólfar in Icelandic) is a stainless-steel sculpture of a ship's skeleton, made by Jón Gunnar Árnason. It sits on a small headland beside the Sæbraut road, with the sea behind it. The long, flowing ribs look light and slightly unreal, as if the boat is drifting. The artist described it as a dreamboat and an ode to the Sun, and he meant it to suggest hope, progress and freedom.

It was made for Reykjavík's 200th anniversary. It won a competition in 1986 and was unveiled on the city's birthday, 18 August 1990. It stands on a circle of granite slabs. The artist knew it would end up facing north rather than west towards the setting sun, and he accepted that.

It photographs well because the shape is simple and stands against open sea and sky, so there is little clutter. Because the ship is open and skeletal, you can often see the water through it. Try a few angles: a wide view that includes the shoreline, a low view looking up, and a close view of the curving steel. Other visitors often stand around the base, so take a moment, wait for a gap, or include a person on purpose to show the size.
text.geographic_location: On the Reykjavík waterfront beside the Sæbraut road, on a small headland between the road and the sea.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Reykjavík, go to the Sæbraut road by the shore. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole ship with sea and sky. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a low, dramatic view, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the steel ribs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Then walk the short distance to the granite circle for closer angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the ship on one of the lines, leaving plenty of sky. Crouch down so the ribs rise against the clouds. For a clean picture, wait until nobody is standing on the base, or include one person deliberately for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steel to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sculpture stays dark and detailed instead of washing out. Try a Live Photo to catch moving clouds or water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or early morning, when the sun is low, gives softer light on the steel. Photograph it at sunset for warm light on the steel.

text.access_note: It is an outdoor sculpture beside the Sæbraut road; check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or works.
claims_not_in_sources: From a point west of the sculpture you see the ship roughly side-on, because it faces north (the sources say it faces north).
The sculpture is an outdoor public artwork that can usually be visited freely at any time.
Visitors often gather around the base, so waiting for a gap in the crowd may be needed.

name: Laugavegur
label: Laugavegur
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Skólavörðustígur' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Laugavegur and Skólavörðustígur (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Laugavegur (Reykjavík)'.
notes: Main shopping street.

text.description:
Laugavegur is the main shopping street of downtown Reykjavík and one of the oldest in the city. The name means 'wash road', because it once led to the hot springs in Laugardalur, where local women took their laundry. The street was built in 1885. Today it is lined with shops, restaurants and bars, and on Friday and Saturday nights it is often busy with people until late.

For photographs, the best place to start is the lower end of Skólavörðustígur, where its rainbow-painted stretch meets Laugavegur. Looking uphill, you see the junction of the two streets, the painted road climbing away from you, and Hallgrímskirkja at the far end. Guides often name this painted section as one of the city's most popular photo spots. It makes a clear, colourful picture, with the street leading your eye to the church.

If you want a second view, look down Laugavegur itself. Colourful, mural-covered shopfronts and everyday street life fill the frame, and late afternoon is a good time for it. Laugavegur is long and runs east to Hlemmur, so the painted junction is the part most visitors mean. Early morning is the quietest time, with the fewest people in your shot. Keep your phone steady against your body, and wait a moment for passers-by to clear the frame.
text.geographic_location: Laugavegur is the main shopping street of downtown Reykjavík and runs a long way east towards Hlemmur. The photo spot is at its start, where the rainbow-painted lower part of Skólavörðustígur meets it, below Hallgrímskirkja.
text.directions_text: From anywhere in downtown Reykjavík, head for the foot of Hallgrímskirkja hill, where Skólavörðustígur meets Laugavegur. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the junction and the painted street. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the buildings and the full width of the street, but keep the church centred so the edges are not stretched. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for pulling Hallgrímskirkja closer at the top of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Laugavegur and Skólavörðustígur (lower end of the rainbow-painted stretch, where it meets Laugavegur, looking uphill). The junction of the two streets with the painted lower section of Skólavörðustígur leading up toward Hallgrímskirkja at the far end. Face uphill. The marked point on Laugavegur lies to the south-east of where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the painted road in the middle, so it leads the eye up to the church. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level so the buildings stand straight. For a different view, walk onto Laugavegur and shoot along the street at the colourful, mural-covered shopfronts and the people passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the painted road to focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky and the church from washing out. Try a Live Photo, so you can pick the frame with the fewest passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is best and there are fewest people. For the view along Laugavegur itself, late afternoon works well.

text.access_note: Both are open public streets; if you plan to visit any particular shop, church or venue nearby, check the official site before you go.

name: Alþingishúsið
label: Parliament House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Austurvöllur' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Austurvöllur' (way/293133747): middle (124 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/110885345: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Alþingishúsið' (43 m across).
notes: Iceland's parliament building beside Austurvöllur.

text.description:
Alþingishúsið is the Parliament House, a calm, classical building in dark stone that sits beside the square of Austurvöllur in central Reykjavík. It still houses Alþingi, the Icelandic parliament. It was designed by Ferdinand Meldahl and built from hewn Icelandic dolerite between 1880 and 1881. Over the years it has also been home to the National Library, the National Gallery, parts of the University of Iceland and, until 1973, the President's offices.

It photographs well because the façade is simple and symmetrical, and the dark stone stands out against the square's lawn and trees. Look up at the first-floor windows: the reliefs above the four outermost ones show the four guardian spirits of Iceland, a dragon, a vulture, a giant and a bull. They make a good detail shot if your phone has a zoom lens.

The best all-round picture is from the lawn of Austurvöllur, facing the building's front. The statue of Jón Sigurðsson makes a good foreground if you want some depth. A second option is Kirkjutorg, which shows more of the surrounding street and square, especially in evening light. Keep clear of the entrances and any security areas, and take a moment to check for people walking across your frame before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: In central Reykjavík, on the edge of the square of Austurvöllur, which is directly in front of the building.
text.directions_text: Head for Austurvöllur in central Reykjavík. Walk across the lawn or paving until the whole front of the building sits comfortably in your screen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the building. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or trees force you to stand close. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the window reliefs and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Austurvöllur (lawn/park on the square directly across from the building's main north façade). The full front façade of the dark basalt Parliament House, framed by the square's trees and lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with the horizontal lines so it looks straight. Hold the phone level and keep the roofline parallel to the top of the screen. Let some lawn and tree branches fill the edges of the frame. For a different view, include the bronze statue of Jón Sigurðsson in the foreground, or try Kirkjutorg for a wider look at the street and square around the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the dark stone keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. If the ultra-wide makes the walls lean inwards, step back and use the default lens (1x) instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light gives clean, even photos of the façade, while late afternoon adds warmer tones to the stone. Weekdays may be busier around the building.

text.access_note: The square in front is an open public space, but entry to the Parliament House itself is not guaranteed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Austurvöllur is an open public square with lawn and trees where visitors can walk freely.
The 0.5x ultra-wide lens can make vertical lines lean inwards when you tilt the phone.
Winter conditions in Reykjavík can make the paving slippery and the square windy.
The building may be busier on weekdays because Parliament is still in session.

name: Statue of Leif Erikson
label: Leif Erikson Statue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hallgrímstorg' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hallgrímstorg' (way/1224997038): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1346965358: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Leifur Ericson' (8 m across).
notes: Statue in front of Hallgrímskirkja.

text.description:
Leif Erikson stands on a tall granite pedestal shaped like the prow of a Viking ship, looking out over the city, with the stepped front and tall tower of Hallgrímskirkja rising directly behind him. That pairing is why the spot works so well on a phone: dark bronze in the foreground, pale church behind, and a clear sky above both.

The statue is by the American sculptor Alexander Stirling Calder. The United States gave it to the people of Iceland to mark the 1,000th anniversary of the Alþingi, the Icelandic parliament, in 1930. It was unveiled on 17 July 1932 on the hill of Skólavörðuholt. The pedestal is about 4.6 metres high, made of Texas red granite, and carries an inscription about the gift.

The best-known view is from Hallgrímstorg, the square in front of the church. Stand close to the base of the pedestal and face the church, so the figure sits in the foreground and the whole height of the façade fits behind him. For a quieter, church-focused alternative, the green garden at the Einar Jónsson Museum gives a side view of Hallgrímskirkja. Another option is to go down Skólavörðustígur and look back up at the statue and plaza, with the street running away towards downtown.

The square can be busy, so allow a little patience for a clear frame. Take a few shots with and without people in them, as visitors also give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: The statue is in central Reykjavik, on the square called Hallgrímstorg on the hill of Skólavörðuholt. It stands directly in front of Hallgrímskirkja.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops for this spot, so start from the centre of Reykjavik and head uphill towards the tall church tower, which is easy to spot. Skólavörðustígur runs up the slope to the square. Once you are the statue is about 1 minute on foot to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the statue and church together. If you can stand a little back, try telephoto (2x or more) so the church looks larger behind the figure. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are right at the pedestal and want the church's full height.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hallgrímstorg (stand right at the base of the pedestal, facing the church). The bronze figure in the foreground with the full height of Hallgrímskirkja's stepped façade and tower rising behind him.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright (portrait) to fit the figure and the tower in one frame, and turn on gridlines to keep the church's vertical lines straight. Tilt the phone as little as you can, or the tower will lean. For something different, try the side view of the church from the Einar Jónsson Museum garden. Or go down Skólavörðustígur and shoot back up at the statue and square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze figure to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the statue does not turn into a silhouette. If your phone has Live Photos or motion, leave it on, as it can help you pick a frame without people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning tends to mean fewer people. Sunset is said to give softer light on the bronze.

text.access_note: The statue stands in an open public square, which is free to visit and open 24 hours.

name: Reykjavík Cathedral
label: Reykjavik Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Austurvöllur' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Austurvöllur' (way/293133747): middle (124 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87377712: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Reykjavík Cathedral' (42 m across).
notes: Small Lutheran cathedral on Austurvöllur square.

text.description:
Reykjavík Cathedral is the seat of the Bishop of Iceland and the mother church of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Iceland. It is also the parish church of the old city centre. It stands on the edge of Austurvöllur, the green square in the middle of town, with the Parliament House (Alþingishúsið) right beside it. That pairing is what makes the view work for a phone: the church, the lawn and the Parliament building all fit into one calm, easy scene that says 'this is central Reykjavík'.

The story gives you something to talk about as you shoot. The first cathedral was built in 1787 to a design by the royal building inspector Andreas Hallander. It was pulled down in 1847 to make way for a somewhat larger church. Since Iceland's parliament, the Alþingi, was revived in 1845, each session has opened with a Mass here, after which the dean leads the members of parliament across to the Parliament House.

The best exterior photo is taken from the open lawn of the square, looking at the cathedral across the grass. Early morning is the suggested time for quieter views. Take one wide shot with the Parliament House beside the church, then a closer one of the church on its own.
text.geographic_location: In the old city centre of Reykjavík, on the edge of the Austurvöllur square, directly beside the Parliament House (Alþingishúsið).
text.directions_text: Head for the old city centre of Reykjavík and look for Austurvöllur, the green square beside the Parliament House. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the lawn to get the cathedral and the Parliament House together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close or want more sky and grass. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the church front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Austurvöllur (open lawn of the square, facing the cathedral). The cathedral framed across the green square, with the Parliament House beside it in the same view. If you want a different angle, walk a little along the grass; the view stays good across the lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the cathedral on one of the vertical lines, with the Parliament House filling the other side. Keep the phone level so the walls stay straight. Include a strip of lawn in the foreground to give depth. For a second shot, zoom in on the cathedral alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail. Keep the phone steady against your body or a rail rather than holding it at arm's length.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is suggested for quieter views and cleaner photos of the surrounding buildings.

text.access_note: Austurvöllur is an open public square, but the cathedral may be closed outside posted hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The cathedral is on the south side of Austurvöllur as seen from the stand-here point (derived from the map data, subject lies south of it).
The cathedral may be closed outside posted hours, and photography is discouraged during services.
Early morning tends to be quieter on the square.

name: Höfði
label: Höfði House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sæbraut' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sæbraut nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/104079936: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hofdi house' (27 m across).
notes: Historic house where Reagan and Gorbachev met in 1986.

text.description:
Höfði is a white timber house on the Reykjavik waterfront, built in 1909 and best known for the 1986 Reykjavík Summit, when Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met here. It was put up for the French consul, Jean-Paul Brillouin, and shows the influence of Jugendstil. The house was prefabricated in Norway, shipped to Iceland and erected on the site. Later the British Embassy used it, and the city bought it in 1958. Since then it has hosted formal receptions. The site also saw Iceland's first radio contact with the outside world, in 1905.

It photographs well because it sits beside the shore, so the sea and the shoreline can lead the eye towards it. The walk along the sea towards the house gives a calm approach shot, which is a good alternative to a close-up. If you want the building itself, the grounds show its white front against the sky. Another option is a wider frame with the open bay and Mount Esja behind it, which gives the house a sense of place.

The inside is generally closed, so plan on photographing from the grounds and public paths, and keep clear of any temporary barriers.
text.geographic_location: Höfði stands on the Reykjavik seafront, beside the Sæbraut waterfront route. Its address is listed as Félagstún or Borgartún, so check on the day.
text.directions_text: Head to the Sæbraut waterfront path and walk the last part along the coast. Höfði sits beside this route. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the approach shot, so the sea, the shoreline and the house all fit in one frame. Use telephoto (2x) if you want the house larger without walking closer. Ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the grounds, if you want a lot of sky above the white front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sæbraut (waterfront walk approaching Höfði from the west). The house seen from the coastal path, with the sea and shoreline leading the eye toward it. It is a quieter spot than the grounds and works best for an approach shot rather than a close-up.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the shoreline along a lower line, with the house on one of the vertical lines. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, walk into the grounds and frame the white timber front against the sky. Another option is the open bay with Mount Esja behind the house.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Phones tend to overexpose white buildings, and a slightly darker frame keeps the detail in the timber.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or evening light is kinder to the white walls than harsh midday sun. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The house itself is generally closed inside, so photograph from the grounds and public paths, respect any temporary barriers, and check the official site before you go.

name: Kolaportið
label: Kolaportið Market
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6691788385: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kolaportið'.
notes: Indoor flea market near the harbour.

text.description: Kolaportið is Iceland's only flea market, and it fills the old Customs building close to the harbour in central Reykjavík. It is a lively place for people photography and for small, colourful details. Stalls sell second-hand records, clothing, antiques, books and liquorice. In the food section, fishmongers sell dried cod, pickled herring and fermented shark, which make good close-up subjects. The market opened in 1989 in the city parking garage under a bank building, then moved into the Customs House in 1994. The building's future has been uncertain: in 2024 the City of Reykjavik decided to move the University of the Arts into it and began a search for new premises for the market. As no suitable site was found, the market was extended to at least March 2025, so check that it is still running before you plan a visit. It is normally open only at weekends. Indoor light can be dim or mixed, so keep your phone steady and look for stalls near doors or bright lamps. Ask before photographing a stallholder or their goods close up. Shoot rows of records, shelves of books or racks of clothing for a sense of the place, then step in for single objects. Be mindful of other visitors, keep your bag close and take care not to block the aisles while you compose your shot.
text.geographic_location: Kolaportið is in the old Customs building by the harbour, in central Reykjavík, close to the harbour.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to the old Customs building by the harbour in central Reykjavík. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so you can photograph as soon as you step inside. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for stalls and aisles, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details like records, jars and food without crowding the stallholder. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can help in a tight aisle, but keep people away from the edges of the frame, where faces can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stay to the side of the aisle so you do not block other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a row of stalls so the aisle leads the eye into the picture. Then move in on one subject, such as a crate of vinyl or a fish counter, and keep the background simple. Portrait mode suits a single object on a table.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your subject to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so bright lamps do not wash out the stalls. If the picture looks dim, turn on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the market is open, normally at weekends.

text.access_note: This is an indoor market that is normally open only at weekends, so check the official site before you go for current dates and times.

name: Reykjavik Old Harbour
label: Old Harbour
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OSM N5830610821 (Reykjavík Old Harbour): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Fishing and whale-watching harbour with colourful boats.

text.description:
Reykjavik Old Harbour is the waterfront spot at number 14 on this map, and it suits a phone camera well because so much sits close together: moored boats, working quaysides, the water itself and the buildings along the edge. You can shoot wide scenes of the whole basin, then step in for small details such as ropes, hulls, painted metal and reflections.

As you approach, take a few frames along the way. Looking back along the quay often gives a different view from the one you aimed for.

For a simple, tidy shot, find a spot where the water fills the lower third of the frame and a line of boats or quayside leads the eye into the picture. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, which matters a lot with open water. If the harbour is busy, wait a moment for people or vehicles to move out of the frame, or use them to give a sense of scale. Wipe your lens first, as sea air and fingerprints soften the picture. Harbours are working places, so keep clear of moving vehicles and boat equipment while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Reykjavik Old Harbour is on the city's waterfront, about 230 metres north-west of the stand-here point.
text.directions_text: It is about 233 m on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view of the harbour. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole basin in one frame, and use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out boats or details across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 230 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line. Use a quay edge or a row of boats as a leading line. Keep the ultra-wide away from the edges of people or objects, which can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boats or buildings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water is bright. Try Live Photos to capture moving water and boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower, usually gives softer light on the water. On a cloudy day, look for colour in the boats and buildings.

text.access_note: The harbour area is a public waterfront, but access to individual quays may vary, so follow any signs on site.
claims_not_in_sources: The Old Harbour is a working waterfront with moored boats, quaysides and buildings along its edge.
Low sun early or late in the day usually gives softer light on water.
Parts of the harbour may be restricted working areas, and vehicles and boat equipment may be moving about.

name: National Gallery of Iceland
label: National Gallery
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/688998282: the OpenStreetMap point 'National Gallery of Iceland'.
notes: Art museum beside Tjörnin.

text.description:
The National Gallery of Iceland is an art museum in Reykjavik that holds a collection of Icelandic art. The main building at Fríkirkjuvegur 7 was erected in 1916 as a freezing plant, designed by the Icelandic architect Guðjón Samúelsson. A later extension is the work of Garðar Halldórsson. The gallery itself dates back to 1884, when it was founded in Copenhagen, and the collection moved to this address in 1987. Today it holds around 16,000 works across three locations. The Fríkirkjuvegur building has exhibition halls on three floors, an art store and a café.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the building's solid shape and its clean lines, which suit a simple, well-balanced picture. A few minutes here gives you a record of the place that you can pair with a shot of the art inside, if photography is allowed in the current exhibition. Rules on photography inside can differ from show to show, so look for signs or ask at the desk. Outside, give yourself a little space, turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the walls with the grid so the building does not look tilted. Take one wide shot to show the whole front, then step closer or zoom in for a detail such as a doorway, a window or the texture of the wall.
text.geographic_location: In Reykjavik, on Fríkirkjuvegur, the street named in the address Fríkirkjuvegur 7. The gallery's offices are nearby on Laufásvegur.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops listed here, so plan to arrive on foot or by road from elsewhere in Reykjavik. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer and the front will not fit, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as windows and doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. This gives you some distance, so the building fits in the frame without needing the widest lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical edges of the walls parallel to the grid lines so the building does not lean. Hold the phone level and, if you like, crouch a little to keep the lines straight. Take one full view, then a tighter one on a detail. Try to keep passers-by out of the edges of the frame or use them for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and the sky does not wash out. Portrait mode is not needed here, but can help if you photograph a person in front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day is kinder to the walls than harsh midday sun. In winter the days are short, so check daylight hours before you go.

text.access_note: The building is a museum with exhibition halls, so entry to the inside may be ticketed and hours may vary; check the official site before you go.

name: Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur
label: Hot Dog Stand
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tryggvagata' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Tryggvagata nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87371096: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (8 m across).
notes: Famous hot dog stand near the harbour.

text.description:
Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur, which translates as "The Town's Best Hot Dogs", is a small hot dog stand on Tryggvagata in central Reykjavik. It is the flagship of a small local chain. It photographs well because it is simple and instantly recognisable: a compact stand, usually with a line of customers in front, set against a busy downtown street. That gives you a real slice of everyday Reykjavik rather than a posed monument.

The chain has been running continuously since 1937, when the first stand opened on Austurstræti. In the 1960s it moved two streets north to Tryggvagata, across from the Harpa Concert Hall, and the main stand is still there. Its profile rose after Bill Clinton visited in 2004, and in 2006 The Guardian named it the best hot dog stand in Europe.

For a phone photo, cross to the far side of Tryggvagata and shoot back at the stand, so the whole front and the queue fit in the frame. The queue can block the view from the pavement at busy times, so be patient and wait for a gap, or step back a little. If you want the Harpa shot too, turn around and take a second photo of the glass building across the road. A small detail such as the stand's sign or someone holding "one with everything" also makes a nice close-up.
text.geographic_location: In central Reykjavik, on Tryggvagata near the harbour, directly across the street from the Harpa Concert Hall. It stands in the downtown area, a short way from Austurstræti, where the first stand opened.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops serve this spot, so start from the town centre and head for the harbour and the Harpa Concert Hall, or go by taxi or hired scooter to Tryggvagata. The stand is on Tryggvagata directly across from Harpa. Once you are on the street, look for the small stand and its queue. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the stand, the queue and some of the street in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back. Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out the sign and the serving hatch from across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tryggvagata (Opposite side of the street from the stand, the side facing Harpa Concert Hall). The stand with the Harpa concert hall's glass facade in the background, taken from across the road. From there the stand is a short way to the south-west, so you are looking back across the road at its front and the queue of customers. Harpa is behind you, so turn round for a second shot of its glass facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the stand on one of the side lines, leaving room for the street and the people queuing. Wait until no one walks directly between you and the stand. You can also take a closer shot of the stand's front and queue as an alternative to the wide view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stand to focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the white sign from looking too bright. Take a short Live Photo if you want the queue and street movement as well.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the queue is short so the stand is easier to see. Daylight is easiest for a clear shot of the sign. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.

text.access_note: This is an open street-side spot on a public road, but the stand itself is a food business, so check the official site before you go for when it is serving.
claims_not_in_sources: Harpa's glass facade should be visible if you turn round and look back across Tryggvagata from the stand-here point.
The queue at the stand can be long at busy times and may block the view from the pavement.
Daylight is generally easiest for a clear photo of the stand's sign.
The stand's opening hours may vary, including late at weekends, so they should be checked before a night visit.

name: Reykjavík City Hall
label: City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tjarnargata' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Tjarnargata nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/89811581: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Reykjavik City Hall' (103 m across).
notes: Modern building rising from the edge of Tjörnin.

text.description: Reykjavík City Hall (Ráðhús Reykjavíkur) sits right beside Tjörnin, the City Pond, in the middle of the city. The building was completed in 1992 after an international competition won by the architects Studio Granda. Inside are the mayor's offices and a large 3D map of Iceland, and the hall is sometimes used for art exhibitions, functions and live music. From outside, it looks like a white-and-grey concrete hall standing on the water. That is why it photographs so well. The pond gives you a reflection, open sky and often swans or ducks for the foreground, and the downtown buildings sit behind. A phone copes well with this kind of scene. The easiest picture is a wide shot along the pond shore, with the hall on one side and the town roofline beyond. If you want something tighter, wait for a bird to drift into the foreground and let the hall sit soft behind it. Walk a little way along the shore too, because the hall's angles and its reflection change as you move. The paths beside the pond can be icy in winter, so watch your footing while you look at the screen.
text.geographic_location: In central Reykjavík, on the edge of the Tjörnin pond, close to Tjarnargata and the downtown buildings.
text.directions_text: Start from central Reykjavík and head for the shore of Tjörnin near Tjarnargata. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full pond, the hall and the downtown buildings together. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the hall. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the reflection or for birds on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tjarnargata (the stretch of pond shore near Tjarnargata, where the City Hall sits). A broad view across the pond that takes in the City Hall alongside the downtown buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line, so the reflection fills the bottom third and the hall sits to one side. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, walk round to Tjörnin itself, where the white-and-grey hall stands on the water with its reflection and the swans or ducks in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale concrete and sky don't turn white. For birds, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Calm, dry days are best, as still water gives the clearest reflection.

text.access_note: Take care on the paths beside the pond, especially in winter.

name: Tjörnin
label: Tjörnin Pond
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fríkirkjuvegur' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Fríkirkjuvegur nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2583093: large area 'Reykjavíkurtjörn' (902 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: City-centre lake with birds and views of the town hall.

text.description:
Tjörnin, whose name simply means "the pond", is a small lake right in the middle of Reykjavik. Most visitors walk along its shore at some point. It is shallow, with an average depth of about half a metre, and it is a haven for birds: between 40 and 50 species of water bird have been recorded here, including Arctic terns, eiders, greylag geese and whooper swans. The modern City Hall stands in the north-west corner and looks as though it is rising out of the water, and several museums and the Dómkirkja cathedral are close by.

It photographs well because open water gives you a calm foreground, with the downtown buildings rising behind it. The east bank, on Fríkirkjuvegur near the white Free Church (Fríkirkjan), gives one of the most balanced views. The water leads your eye towards the skyline, and the church and the nearby gallery add colour along the shore. If you have time, City Hall reflected in the water is a good second picture, and the park on the southern edge (Hljómskálagarðurinn) gives a greener, more natural view.

In winter the pond usually freezes from time to time and is used for skating, which changes the scene and can limit how close you can get to the water's edge. Check conditions before you go. Take a few frames with birds in the foreground for a bit of life in the picture.
text.geographic_location: Tjörnin lies in the centre of Reykjavik, next to the City Hall in its north-west corner and close to several museums. The Hljómskálagarðurinn park runs along its southern end.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the city centre by the City Hall and the pond, then walk round to the eastern shore. Walk to Fríkirkjuvegur, by the Free Church, on the east side of the pond. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of water, church and skyline. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and shoreline. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out City Hall or the birds without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Fríkirkjuvegur (east bank, near Fríkirkjan church). Open water in the foreground with the city rising behind the pond, framed by the white Free Church on the eastern shore. The exact spot may vary along the street, so walk a few steps either way until the water fills the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon of the far shore on the upper third line, so the water takes up most of the picture. Keep the church at one edge as a frame. For a different picture, City Hall reflected in the water works well from its own side of the pond, and Hljómskálagarðurinn gives a greener view with grass along the shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. When birds come close, tap on them to focus and take a few quick shots, or try a Live Photo to catch the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Calm, bright conditions give the clearest reflections on the water. In winter, check whether the pond has frozen, as the scene looks quite different and the water's edge may be harder to reach.

text.access_note: This is an open public shoreline and street, but if the pond is frozen, access to the water's edge may be limited, so check conditions before you go.

Looking west from the east bank, the water and skyline are lit from the side or front depending on the time of day.

text.description: Fríkirkjan í Reykjavík, the Free Church, is a Lutheran church that stands independently of the Church of Iceland. It sits in the centre of the city on the east side of the lake Tjörnin, which makes it an easy stop on a walk around the water. The congregation was founded in the autumn of 1899, and the church was consecrated on 22 February 1903. It was lengthened only two years later, then enlarged again in 1924, when a concrete chancel was added at the eastern end. For a photograph, the church is a simple, clear shape that stands out well against the open space near the lake, and the water gives you a calm foreground when the surface is still. Start with a wide view that shows the church and a little of its surroundings. Then move in for a tighter shot of the entrance and the front of the building. Keep your phone level so the walls stay straight, and wait a moment for passers-by to clear if you want a clean view. If you want to go inside, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Reykjavik, on the eastern side of the lake Tjörnin. The church stands right beside the water, close to the city's central streets.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot. Start from the lake Tjörnin in the city centre and walk to the east side of the lake. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole church from where you stand. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the front, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you step closer and want to fit everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From here the whole building should sit comfortably in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the church up with the vertical lines so the walls stay straight. Leave a little space around it so the building does not touch the edge of the picture. If the lake is near and the water is calm, try including some of it in the lower part of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Take a few frames in a row, as people and cars move through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters buildings and brings out their shape. Calm, still days are best for reflections in the lake nearby.

text.access_note: The surroundings are an outdoor public area, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside the church.

name: Austurvöllur
label: Austurvöllur Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Austurvöllur' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/293133747: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Austurvöllur' (124 m across).
notes: Central square in front of the parliament.

text.description:
Austurvöllur is a public square in central Reykjavik, and it is an easy place to take a good phone photo. The grass is surrounded by cafés, and the square is dominated by a large statue of Jón Sigurðsson, a leader of Iceland's independence movement. Behind the statue stands the Parliament House (Alþingishúsið), and nearby is Dómkirkjan, the city's oldest church. That makes a tidy picture: a person, a building and a bit of history in a single frame.

The square has not always looked like this. In the early 18th century it was much larger, and for a long time a statue of Bertel Thorvaldsen stood where Jón Sigurðsson stands now. It has also been a regular place for protests, because Parliament is so close.

For the classic photo, stand in the middle of the square and point your phone so the statue is in the foreground and Parliament sits behind it. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines to keep the Parliament House straight. Go early if you can, before about 10 a.m., when the lawn is quieter. If you turn around and look across the city, Hallgrímskirkja shows up in the distance. It is a nice second shot, best taken with the zoom.
text.geographic_location: Austurvöllur is in the old centre of Reykjavik, beside the Parliament House and Dómkirkjan. It is surrounded by Vallarstræti, Pósthússtræti, Kirkjustræti and Thorvaldsensstræti.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or train stops for this spot, so head for the old centre of Reykjavik, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Ask for Austurvöllur, the square beside the Parliament House. Once there, walk to the middle of the square, where the phone icon on the map is. If you are already in the town centre, the square is only a short stroll away. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with Parliament behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the buildings around it. For Hallgrímskirkja in the distance, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows Jón Sigurðsson's statue in the foreground with the Parliament House (Alþingishúsið) behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the statue in the foreground and let Parliament fill the background. Turn on gridlines and line up the Parliament House with a horizontal line so it looks straight. Keep the phone steady and level, and crouch slightly if you want the statue to stand out more against the building. For a different view, you can also shoot towards Hallgrímskirkja from within the green space.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework and the statue do not turn washed-out. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 10 a.m., when the lawn is quieter and the light is better for the statue and Parliament.

text.access_note: Austurvöllur is a free, open public square, but it is sometimes used for gatherings and protests, so check for gatherings or protests before you go if you need a clear view on a particular day.
